title: Vectors & Matrices
description: The building blocks of AI math: what vectors and matrices are, and how to add, scale, and multiply them

lessons.title: What is a Vector?
lessons.description: See a vector as a list of numbers with a direction and size, and add/scale them

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Explain what a vector is, add two vectors, and scale a vector by a number.

sections.title: ➡️ A vector is just a list of numbers
sections.content:
In AI, a **vector** is simply an ordered list of numbers — nothing mysterious. A customer's `[age, income, purchases]` is a vector. A word's meaning, encoded by a language model, is a vector. A pixel's RGB color is a vector of length 3.

```python
customer = [25, 52000, 14]   # age, income, purchases
color = [255, 0, 128]        # red, green, blue
```

Geometrically, a vector also has a picture: an arrow from the origin pointing to that list of coordinates. Both views — 'a list of numbers' and 'an arrow in space' — are the same thing, and you'll switch between them depending on what's easier to reason about.

sections.title: ➕ Adding vectors
sections.content:
Vectors of the same length add **element by element**:

```python
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
b = np.array([4, 5, 6])
print(a + b)   # [5 7 9]
```

Picture it as placing one arrow's tail at the other's tip — the result points from the very start to the very end. This shows up constantly: averaging several vectors, combining feature contributions, or accumulating gradient updates are all vector addition underneath.

sections.title: ✖️ Scaling a vector
sections.content:
Multiplying a vector by a single number (a **scalar**) stretches or shrinks every element by that same amount:

```python
v = np.array([2, 4, 6])
print(v * 3)     # [ 6 12 18] — stretched to 3x the length
print(v * 0.5)   # [1. 2. 3.] — shrunk to half the length
print(v * -1)    # [-2 -4 -6] — same length, opposite direction
```

Scaling by a negative number keeps the same length but flips the direction — this is exactly why gradient descent (a later module) moves *opposite* the gradient: it scales the gradient vector by a negative learning rate.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content: Trying to add two vectors of different lengths — this isn't defined, and NumPy will raise an error rather than guess what you meant. Confusing a vector (an arrow, or list of numbers) with a single number (a scalar) — they behave differently under multiplication, as you just saw.

questions.question: What is a vector, in the simplest terms?
options: A single number
An ordered list of numbers, which can also be pictured as an arrow
A table with rows and columns
A type of loop in Python
questions.explanation: A vector is an ordered list of numbers — you can treat it as raw data (a list) or picture it geometrically as an arrow pointing from the origin.

questions.question: What does np.array([1, 2]) + np.array([3, 4]) return?
options: An error, since vectors can't be added
questions.explanation: Vector addition combines elements at matching positions: 1+3=4 and 2+4=6, giving [4, 6].

questions.question: What happens when you multiply a vector by -1?
options: Every element becomes zero
The vector's length doubles
Its direction flips, but its length stays the same
It becomes a scalar
questions.explanation: Multiplying by -1 negates every element, which points the arrow in exactly the opposite direction while leaving its length unchanged.

questions.question: What does np.array([5, 5]) - np.array([2, 1]) return?
options: An error, since vectors can't be subtracted
questions.explanation: Vector subtraction happens element-by-element, just like addition: [5-2, 5-1] = [3, 4].

questions.question: What determines the number of dimensions a vector has?
options: Its length (magnitude)
How many numbers it contains
Whether it points up or down
Whether it's positive or negative
questions.explanation: A vector's dimensionality is simply how many numbers (components) it holds — [1, 2, 3] is a 3-dimensional vector.

questions.question: What happens when you multiply a vector by 2?
options: Its direction flips
Every element doubles, stretching the vector to twice its length in the same direction
It becomes a matrix
Only the first element changes
questions.explanation: Multiplying a vector by a positive scalar scales every element by that amount, stretching (or shrinking) it while keeping the same direction.

questions.question: In machine learning, what can a vector represent besides a geometric arrow?
options: Only physical direction and speed
A list of features describing a single data point, like [height, weight, age]
A single probability value
A type of loop
questions.explanation: In ML, vectors commonly represent feature sets for a data point — each number in the vector is one measured attribute.

questions.question: What is the zero vector, and what happens when you add it to any vector v?
options: A vector with no elements; adding it causes an error
A vector of all zeros; adding it leaves v completely unchanged
The vector [1, 1, ..., 1]; adding it doubles v
It only exists in 2D
questions.explanation: The zero vector has every component equal to 0, so adding it to any vector v leaves v exactly as it was.

lessons.title: Dot Products & Vector Length
lessons.description: Combine two vectors into one number with the dot product, and measure a vector's length

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Compute a dot product and a vector's length (norm), and explain what the dot product measures.

sections.title: 🔗 The dot product: combining two vectors into one number
sections.content:
The **dot product** multiplies two vectors' matching elements together, then adds up the results — turning two vectors into a single number:

```python
a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
b = np.array([4, 5, 6])
print(a.dot(b))   # 1*4 + 2*5 + 3*6 = 32
```

This shows up everywhere in AI: a neural network layer is, at its core, a bunch of dot products between an input vector and each neuron's weight vector.

sections.title: 📏 Vector length (the norm)
sections.content:
A vector's **length** (also called its **norm**) tells you how big it is — how far its arrow reaches. It's computed as the square root of the vector dotted with itself:

```python
v = np.array([3, 4])
print(np.linalg.norm(v))   # 5.0
```

This is just the Pythagorean theorem generalized to any number of dimensions: √(3² + 4²) = √25 = 5. You'll see this used to measure how large a set of weights or an error vector has gotten.

sections.title: 🧭 What the dot product actually measures
sections.content:
The dot product captures **how aligned two vectors are**, not just their raw values:

• A large positive dot product → the vectors point in a similar direction
• A dot product near zero → the vectors are roughly perpendicular (unrelated)
• A negative dot product → the vectors point in somewhat opposite directions

This is exactly the intuition behind **cosine similarity**, which you'll meet again when this course reaches embeddings: two ideas 'mean similar things' when their vector representations have a large dot product relative to their lengths.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content: Forgetting the two vectors need the same length for a dot product to make sense. Assuming a large dot product always means 'similar' without accounting for vector length — two long vectors pointing in slightly different directions can have a bigger dot product than two short, perfectly aligned ones.

questions.question: What does np.array([1, 0]).dot(np.array([0, 1])) equal, and what does that suggest?
options: 2, meaning the vectors are very similar
0, meaning the vectors are perpendicular — unrelated in direction
1, meaning the vectors are identical
An error, since dot products require identical vectors
questions.explanation: 1*0 + 0*1 = 0. A dot product of zero indicates the two vectors are perpendicular, i.e. they share no directional overlap.

questions.question: What is np.linalg.norm(v) computing?
options: The sum of v's elements
The length (magnitude) of vector v
The number of elements in v
The dot product of v with itself, without the square root
questions.explanation: norm() computes the vector's length — the square root of the sum of its squared elements, generalizing the Pythagorean theorem.

questions.question: What does a large positive dot product between two vectors generally suggest?
options: The vectors are unrelated
The vectors point in a similar direction
The vectors are exactly equal
One vector must be the zero vector
questions.explanation: A large positive dot product indicates strong alignment — the vectors tend to point in a similar direction, which is the intuition behind measuring similarity between things represented as vectors.

questions.question: How is the dot product of two vectors [a, b] and [c, d] computed?
options: a + b + c + d
a*c + b*d
(a*c, b*d)
max(a, c) + max(b, d)
questions.explanation: The dot product multiplies corresponding elements and sums the results: for [a,b]·[c,d], that's a*c + b*d.

questions.question: What does the dot product of a vector with itself (v · v) relate to?
options: Its direction only
The square of its length (norm)
Always zero
Whether it's the zero vector
questions.explanation: v · v sums the squares of v's components, which is exactly the squared length of v — so np.linalg.norm(v) is the square root of v.dot(v).

questions.question: What does a negative dot product between two vectors suggest?
options: The vectors are identical
The vectors point in roughly opposite directions
One vector must be the zero vector
The vectors are perpendicular
questions.explanation: A negative dot product indicates the angle between the vectors is greater than 90 degrees — they point in broadly opposite directions.

questions.question: What is a unit vector?
options: Any vector with only one element
A vector with length (norm) exactly 1
A vector where every element equals 1
The zero vector
questions.explanation: A unit vector is one whose magnitude is exactly 1 — you get one by dividing a vector by its own norm.

questions.question: How is cosine similarity between two vectors related to their dot product?
options: They're unrelated concepts
Cosine similarity is the dot product divided by the product of the vectors' lengths, isolating the angle between them
Cosine similarity is always equal to the dot product
Cosine similarity only works for vectors of length 1
questions.explanation: Cosine similarity normalizes the dot product by both vectors' lengths, so it measures only the angle (direction similarity) regardless of magnitude.

lessons.title: What is a Matrix?
lessons.description: See a matrix as a table of numbers, and understand matrix-vector multiplication as a transformation

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Read a matrix's shape, and explain what matrix-vector multiplication does geometrically.

sections.title: 🗃️ A matrix is a table of numbers
sections.content:
A **matrix** is a rectangular grid of numbers, arranged in rows and columns. A dataset — rows of examples, columns of features — is exactly a matrix. An image, before any AI touches it, is a matrix of pixel brightness values.

```python
M = np.array([
    [1, 2, 3],
    [4, 5, 6],
])
print(M.shape)   # (2, 3) — 2 rows, 3 columns
```

A matrix's **shape** is always (rows, columns) — worth memorizing that order, since it trips people up constantly.

sections.title: 🔄 Matrix-vector multiplication: applying a transformation
sections.content:
Multiplying a matrix by a vector produces a new vector — think of the matrix as a machine that **transforms** one vector into another:

```python
M = np.array([
    [2, 0],
    [0, 3],
])
v = np.array([1, 1])
print(M @ v)   # [2 3]
```

This particular matrix stretches the x-direction by 2 and the y-direction by 3. Every layer of a neural network, at its core, multiplies an input vector by a weight matrix — that's the machine transforming the input into a new representation.

sections.title: 📐 Shapes must line up
sections.content:
Matrix-vector multiplication only works when the shapes match up correctly: a matrix with shape `(rows, cols)` can only multiply a vector with `cols` elements, and the result has `rows` elements.

```python
# M has shape (2, 3): 2 rows, 3 columns
# v must have exactly 3 elements to match
M = np.array([[1, 0, 1], [0, 1, 1]])
v = np.array([1, 2, 3])
print(M @ v)   # shape (2,) — one number per row of M
```

Getting the shapes to 'line up' is one of the most common everyday tasks when building models — and one of the most common sources of bugs.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content: Mixing up rows and columns when reading a shape — remember it's always (rows, columns). Multiplying a matrix by a vector of the wrong length, which NumPy will refuse with a shape-mismatch error rather than silently guessing.

questions.question: For a matrix with shape (3, 5), what does that tell you?
options: 3 columns and 5 rows
3 rows and 5 columns
It has 15 total elements arranged in a single line
It can only hold whole numbers
questions.explanation: Matrix shapes are always given as (rows, columns), so (3, 5) means 3 rows and 5 columns.

questions.question: What does multiplying a matrix by a vector conceptually do?
options: Adds a new row to the matrix
Transforms the vector into a new vector, according to the matrix
Always returns the same vector unchanged
Deletes elements from the vector
questions.explanation: A matrix acts like a transformation machine: multiplying it by a vector produces a new vector, often stretched, rotated, or otherwise reshaped compared to the original.

questions.question: If M has shape (4, 2), how many elements must a vector v have for M @ v to work?
questions.explanation: The number of columns in M (2) must match the number of elements in v, since each row of M is dotted with v to produce one output value.

questions.question: How can a matrix be thought of in terms of vectors?
options: As a single very long vector
As a collection of row vectors stacked together (or equivalently, column vectors side by side)
Matrices have nothing to do with vectors
As the dot product of two vectors
questions.explanation: A matrix can be viewed as multiple row vectors stacked on top of each other, or equivalently multiple column vectors placed side by side.

questions.question: What makes a matrix 'square'?
options: It contains only whole numbers
It has the same number of rows as columns
It has more rows than columns
It has exactly one row
questions.explanation: A square matrix has an equal number of rows and columns, like shape (4, 4).

questions.question: What is the identity matrix, conceptually?
options: A matrix full of zeros
A special square matrix with 1s on the diagonal and 0s elsewhere, which leaves vectors unchanged when multiplied
Any matrix with the same shape as another
A matrix that always transforms vectors to zero
questions.explanation: The identity matrix has 1s along its diagonal and 0s everywhere else; multiplying any vector by it returns that exact same vector.

questions.question: Why are matrices useful for representing an entire dataset?
options: They can only store a single number
Each row can represent one data point (as a feature vector), so the whole matrix represents many data points at once
Matrices can't hold numeric data
They're only used for images
questions.explanation: Stacking each data point's feature vector as a row produces a matrix that represents an entire dataset in one structure.

questions.question: In matrix notation, what does the entry M[i][j] typically refer to?
options: The value in column i, row j
The value in row i, column j
The sum of row i and column j
The transpose of the matrix
questions.explanation: By standard convention, M[i][j] refers to the entry in row i and column j of the matrix.

lessons.title: Matrix Multiplication
lessons.description: Multiply two matrices together, and see why the order you multiply in matters

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Multiply two compatible matrices, check whether two matrices can be multiplied, and explain why order matters.

sections.title: 🧮 Multiplying two matrices
sections.content:
Matrix-matrix multiplication is matrix-vector multiplication applied repeatedly — each row of the result comes from combining a row of the first matrix with a column of the second:

```python
A = np.array([
    [1, 2],
    [3, 4],
])
B = np.array([
    [5, 6],
    [7, 8],
])
print(A @ B)
# [[19 22]
#  [43 50]]
```

Each entry in the result is a dot product: the top-left `19` comes from `[1, 2] · [5, 7] = 1*5 + 2*7 = 19` — row 1 of A, column 1 of B.

sections.title: 📏 The shape rule: inner dimensions must match
sections.content:
Two matrices can only be multiplied if the **first matrix's number of columns equals the second matrix's number of rows**. The result's shape takes the outer dimensions:

```python
# A: (2, 3)   B: (3, 4)
#        ^match^
# Result: (2, 4)
```

This exact rule is why neural network layers have to be built with compatible shapes — a layer expecting a 128-dimensional input can't be fed a 64-dimensional vector, and this is precisely the shape rule showing up.

sections.title: 🔀 Order matters: A @ B ≠ B @ A
sections.content:
Unlike ordinary number multiplication, matrix multiplication is **not commutative** — swapping the order usually gives a completely different result, and often isn't even possible if the shapes don't line up the other way:

```python
A = np.array([[1, 2], [0, 1]])
B = np.array([[0, 1], [1, 0]])
print(A @ B)   # [[2 1] [1 0]]
print(B @ A)   # [[0 1] [1 2]]  -- different!
```

This is why, when reading model architecture code, the order weight matrices and inputs are multiplied in is never arbitrary — swapping it changes the computation entirely.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content: Assuming matrix multiplication works like regular multiplication and can be reordered freely — it can't. Forgetting to check the shape rule before multiplying, leading to a shape-mismatch error that can be confusing to debug without understanding the rule.

questions.question: For A @ B to be valid, what must be true about their shapes?
options: A and B must have identical shapes
A's number of columns must equal B's number of rows
A and B must both be square matrices
There's no restriction — any two matrices can be multiplied
questions.explanation: The 'inner' dimensions must match: A's column count has to equal B's row count for the multiplication to be defined.

questions.question: Is A @ B always equal to B @ A for matrices?
options: Yes, always
No — matrix multiplication is generally not commutative, and the two can give very different results
Only for square matrices
Only when both matrices contain positive numbers
questions.explanation: Matrix multiplication order matters. Unlike multiplying ordinary numbers, A @ B and B @ A are usually different (and B @ A may not even be valid if the shapes don't line up).

questions.question: If A has shape (2, 3) and B has shape (3, 5), what is the shape of A @ B?
options: This can't be multiplied
questions.explanation: The inner dimensions (3 and 3) match, so the multiplication is valid, and the result takes the outer dimensions: 2 rows from A, 5 columns from B.

questions.question: Is matrix multiplication (A @ B) the same as multiplying corresponding elements together?
options: Yes, they're identical operations
No — matrix multiplication combines rows and columns via dot products, unlike simple element-wise multiplication
Only for square matrices
Only when one matrix is the identity matrix
questions.explanation: Matrix multiplication computes each output entry as a dot product of a row and a column, which is fundamentally different from multiplying matching elements directly (element-wise multiplication).

questions.question: Is matrix multiplication associative, i.e. does (A @ B) @ C equal A @ (B @ C)?
options: No, grouping always changes the result
Yes, as long as the shapes are compatible
Only for 2x2 matrices
Only when A equals B
questions.explanation: Matrix multiplication is associative: as long as the shapes line up, you can group the multiplications in either order and get the same result.

questions.question: What happens when you multiply any matrix M by the identity matrix I (M @ I)?
options: The result is always the zero matrix
The result is M itself, unchanged
The result is I, regardless of M
It's undefined
questions.explanation: The identity matrix acts like the number 1 does in regular multiplication — multiplying by it leaves the other matrix unchanged.

questions.question: How is a single entry of the product matrix A @ B computed?
options: By adding the corresponding entries of A and B
By taking the dot product of the relevant row of A and column of B
By picking the larger of the two matching entries
By dividing A's row sum by B's column sum
questions.explanation: Each entry (i, j) in A @ B is the dot product of A's i-th row and B's j-th column.

questions.question: Why does the order of matrix multiplication matter when passing data through neural network layers?
options: It doesn't matter — layers can be applied in any order
Because each layer's weight matrix transforms its input in a specific sequence, and swapping the order generally produces a different transformation entirely
Because matrices can only be multiplied once
Because neural networks don't actually use matrix multiplication
questions.explanation: Since matrix multiplication is not commutative, applying layer transformations in a different order produces a different overall computation — the sequence matters.
